title: Opening a cafe? Be profitable before you're famous
summary: Don't chase being known, unique or expensive. Chase profit, one cup at a time; the fame follows a cafe that makes money.
body:
*For anyone about to open a cafe. About 7 minutes to read.*

A **profitable cafe** is one that pays its rent, its staff, its suppliers and its owner from its own sales, every single month.

That sounds obvious, yet most new cafes are planned around something else. We plan to be known: the launch reel, the influencer table, the queue on opening weekend. We plan to be unique: the neon sign, the imported chairs, the 40-item menu nobody else has. And to pay for all of it, we plan to be expensive: a Rs 450 cold brew on a street where the chai stall next door charges Rs 20.

This post argues the opposite order. Don't chase being known, don't chase being unique, and don't hide behind a premium price. Chase profit, one cup at a time. The fame, the brand and the second outlet follow a cafe that makes money; they rarely rescue one that doesn't.

## Three things new cafes chase instead of profit

**Being known.** Fame brings the first visit, and the first visit is the cheapest thing a cafe ever gets. About 85 of every 100 first-time guests never come back, and only 3 become regulars ([Bloom Intelligence](https://bloomintelligence.com/blog/first-time-restaurant-guests-return-rate/), US data). A typical cafe needs around 825 regulars to stay open, which at that rate takes about 27,500 first visits, while a strong launch reel might bring 3,000. e.g. Noida's cafe strip filled with photogenic openings, and many closed within months ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/feature/noida-prefers-cafe-culture-restaurants-and-bars-keep-shutting-down/2040122/), 2024). Hence being known fills the cafe for a month; it does not pay the rent for a year.

**Being unique.** Uniqueness is usually bought with money that should have gone into the coffee. The photo wall, the custom furniture and the long menu all raise setup cost and wastage, and none of them is why a guest comes back on a Tuesday. Guests outside the metros say as much: 63% of regular tier-2 coffee drinkers rate taste first ([Restaurant India, citing Coffee Board-CRISIL](https://www.restaurantindia.in/article/how-coffee-is-moving-beyond-metros.17030), 2026). e.g. Corridor Seven in Nagpur has not spent on advertising since 2018; it grew on coffee and cupping sessions, not on looking different ([Fresh Cup](https://freshcup.com/how-indias-smaller-cities-are-rewriting-the-rules-of-specialty-coffee-expansion/), 2026). Thus the cafe that is good every day beats the cafe that is different once.

**Being overpriced.** A premium price often isn't a strategy; it is a way of covering costs that were too high from the start, such as expensive rent and expensive interiors. Guests notice, visit once for the photo and then go back to their usual place. e.g. Even Tata Starbucks, with the strongest coffee brand in the world, saw its loss widen to Rs 135.7 crore in FY25 ([Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/corporate/tata-starbucks-fy25-losses-widen-to-rs-1357-crore-revenue-rises-5-to-rs-1277-crore), 2025), and has had to add cheaper drinks ([Deccan Herald](https://www.deccanherald.com/business/starbucks-india-brews-up-cheaper-drinks-as-domestic-rivals-expand-1225599.html)) and move to smaller, cheaper stores ([Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/corporate/starbucks-asked-to-cut-costs-in-india-as-tatas-halt-fresh-investments)). Hence if a global brand cannot hold a premium price in India, a new cafe with no brand cannot either.

All three share one flaw. They spend money before the cafe has earned any, on the hope that attention will turn into income. It usually doesn't, because attention brings first visits and only a good, fairly priced cup brings the second.

## What profit-first looks like

The easiest way to see a cafe's profit is to follow Rs 100 of sales. Roughly Rs 20 goes to the landlord, Rs 25 to 35 to coffee, milk and food, Rs 25 to 30 to staff, and the rest to power, consumables and repairs, leaving about Rs 10 for us ([Restaurant India](https://www.restaurantindia.in/article/cafe-business-in-india-setup-cost-profit-margins-what-nobody-tells-you.16054), 2026). That Rs 10 is the whole business. Every choice we make either protects it or gives it away.

**Rent comes first.** We keep rent under 20% of honest revenue, the revenue the street can actually deliver, not the revenue we hope for. In our worked example, letting rent creep to 25% stretches the payback from under four years to over seven. e.g. A 1,000 sq ft cafe on Indiranagar's 100 Feet Road needs about 179 bills a day to keep rent at 20%; the same cafe on a Lucknow high street needs about 67 ([Cushman & Wakefield](https://assets.cushmanwakefield.com/-/media/cw/marketbeat-pdfs/2026/q3/apac-and-gc/bengaluru-retail-q3-2026.pdf?rev=50b06e88da194a1993c7f4776a06ec74), 2026; CBRE, 2022). Hence the right street is the one the cafe can carry, not the one that looks best on Instagram.

**Price for the street, not for the interiors.** A fair price is one a regular can pay four times a month without thinking about it. If the numbers only work at a premium price, the problem is usually the rent or the setup cost, and the fix is there, not on the menu. e.g. Chaayos built 200+ cafes around an everyday chai habit and reached an 11.9% EBITDA margin in FY25 ([Entrackr](https://entrackr.com/fintrackr/chaayos-crosses-rs-300-cr-revenue-in-fy25-ebitda-jumps-65x-11088950), 2025). Thus an affordable cup sold often beats an expensive cup sold once.

**Spend on the second visit, not the first.** A small menu we can make well, staff who remember names, and a simple way to take a guest's number and invite them back cost less than one influencer campaign. A simple thank-you message after the visit brought back 29.9% of the guests who received it, against 0.27% for a one-off promotional blast ([Bloom Intelligence](https://bloomintelligence.com/blog/restaurant-customer-retention-2026-guide/), 2026, US vendor data). Hence the cheapest marketing a cafe has is the guest who already came once.

**Grow only when the first cafe pays.** This is where success really does follow profit. Third Wave Coffee had about 70% of its stores losing money in FY24; it stopped, fixed each store until over 90% were EBITDA positive, and only then opened its 250th cafe, in Lucknow ([The Ken](https://the-ken.com/story/inside-third-wave-coffees-unending-reinvention/); [Restaurant India](https://www.restaurantindia.in/news/third-wave-coffee-opens-250th-caf-in-lucknow-targets-320-outlets-by-fy27.n17309), 2026). e.g. Barista, long written off, found that its tier-2 stores make more money than its metro ones, and is now opening 50 to 60 cafes a year, with its 500th in Patna ([Restaurant India](https://www.restaurantindia.in/news/restaurant-india-news-barista-coffee-targets-800-900-stores-by-2030-eyes-tier-ii-iii-towns-for.n15095), 2026). Thus profit came first in both stories, and the fame and the growth came after.

> Fame fills a cafe for a month. Profit keeps it open long enough to become famous.

## Before you sign the lease

We would ask five questions, and we would not sign until each one has an honest answer.

1. **Rent:** is it under 20% of the revenue this street can realistically deliver?
2. **Price:** could a regular afford to come four times a month?
3. **Setup:** would the cafe pay back its setup cost within three to four years at a slow month's sales?
4. **Second visit:** what exactly brings a first-time guest back within 30 days?
5. **Reserve:** do we have three months of fixed costs in the bank, untouched by the launch budget?

If any answer is no, the fix is cheaper now than after the paint dries. A cafe that answers all five may never trend online, but it will still be open next year, and the year after. Thus profit is not the opposite of success; for a cafe, it is the only road to it.

*If you want the full working, the toolkit booklet explains each framework behind these questions, and the case study booklet shows them at work in Third Wave, Cafe Coffee Day, Starbucks and Barista. Figures marked as examples are illustrations built on the sourced benchmarks.*
